theme: Joshua’s farewell; covenant renewal, choose this day
readingInstruction: Read Joshua 23:1-24:33. The book closes with two farewell speeches and a covenant ceremony. Read chapter 23 as an old man’s pastoral warning, and chapter 24 as one of the great covenant renewals in the Bible. Note the question at the center: “Choose this day whom you will serve.”
settingTheScene: Joshua is old, and he knows he will die soon. Like Moses before him, he gathers Israel to give them final instructions. The first speech, in chapter 23, is to the leaders. It is a mixture of reminder and warning. The second, in chapter 24, takes place at Shechem, the place where God first gave Abraham the promise of the land, and where Israel had pronounced the blessings and curses. Joshua retells the story from Abraham to the present and then calls the people to a decision. This is the book’s climax, and it explains what everything has been for. God has kept his promises. Will his people keep faith with him?
observation: Joshua says, “You have seen all that the LORD your God has done… for it is the LORD your God who has fought for you” (23:3).
“Be very strong to keep and to do all that is written in the Book of the Law of Moses” (23:6).
He warns against intermarrying with the nations and serving their gods, for “they shall be a snare and a trap for you” (23:12-13).
At Shechem, Joshua recounts the history from Terah and Abraham, who “served other gods” beyond the River, up to the conquest (24:2-13).
“Now therefore fear the LORD and serve him in sincerity and in faithfulness. Put away the gods that your fathers served” (24:14).
“Choose this day whom you will serve… But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD” (24:15).
The people say, “Far be it from us that we should forsake the LORD,” and Joshua replies, “You are not able to serve the LORD, for he is a holy God” (24:16-19).
Joshua sets up a stone as a witness, and the book ends with the burials of Joshua, Joseph’s bones, and Eleazar (24:26-33).
interpretation:
Joshua’s farewell has the weight of a last testament. He reminds the leaders that the victories were God’s: “it is the LORD your God who has fought for you.” Then he issues a conditional warning. If they cling to the LORD, the nations will be driven out. If they turn aside and join the nations, they will be a snare and a trap, and they will perish from the good land. The word “if” is a reminder that enjoying the inheritance requires faithfulness. The relationship is a covenant, and covenants have promises and responsibilities.

The scene at Shechem is the great moment. Joshua recites the history of salvation: God took Abraham from idolatrous Mesopotamia, gave him a family, delivered them from Egypt, defeated the Amorites, and gave them a land they did not labor for and cities they did not build. It is a summary of grace. Everything the people have is a gift. Then the “therefore” comes. Because God has done all this, fear him and serve him. Obedience in the Bible is always a response to grace.

Then the famous verse. “Choose this day whom you will serve.” It is not a neutral invitation. Joshua presents the options bluntly: the gods beyond the river, the gods of the Amorites, or the LORD. There is no fourth option of serving no one. Everyone worships something. Then he gives his own testimony: “But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.” The decision is personal and also household-wide. A leader’s faith carries weight in his family.

The people respond confidently, but Joshua’s next statement is startling: “You are not able to serve the LORD, for he is a holy God.” This is not discouragement but realism. The people are overconfident. They think they can serve God by their own resolution. Joshua knows that a holy God demands more than good intentions. The law cannot make anyone holy. This is the very question the New Testament will answer. God provides in Christ what the law demanded, and by his Spirit he writes the law on our hearts. We are not able. He is.

The covenant is renewed with a stone as witness. The book ends with burials, a note of closure. Joseph’s bones, carried from Egypt for four hundred years, are finally laid to rest at Shechem. The promise made to him in Genesis 50:25 has been kept. And Joshua dies, called “the servant of the LORD,” a title previously given only to Moses. The next book will show what happens when the leader is gone.
connection: Joshua 24 echoes the covenant formats of Deuteronomy and the ancient suzerainty treaties. The history from Abraham to the conquest summarizes Genesis through Joshua. The burial of Joseph’s bones fulfills Genesis 50:24-25 and Exodus 13:19. The warning about intermarriage recalls Deuteronomy 7:1-4. The inability to serve a holy God anticipates Romans 8:3, Hebrews 10, and Jeremiah 31. Jesus quotes the spirit of this choice in Matthew 6:24, “You cannot serve God and money.”
application:
Take Joshua’s question seriously: whom are you serving? Not in theory, but in practice. Look at where your time, money, and attention flow. Is there a “god” that has quietly taken a throne in your heart? Name it, and renounce it.

Make the household decision. If you have a spouse, children, or roommates, ask what “as for me and my house” might look like in practice: a shared meal and a prayer, a habit of reading Scripture together, a commitment to a church.

Finally, receive the sober words of verse 19. You are not able to serve God in your own strength. Say that honestly to him, and then rely on the Spirit and on Christ’s righteousness to be what you cannot be on your own.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what you choose today, and who you want to serve with.
Ask him to show you any idols you still keep and to give strength to put them away.
Pray for your household or those closest to you.
